t: Minimum Number of Operations to Make X and Y Equal
o: From x you may divide by 11 or 5 (when divisible), or step ±1, minimizing operations to reach y. Direct stepping is O(|x−y|) but divisions leap dramatically. Key observation: when x > y, an optimal strategy soon reaches a multiple of 11 or 5 near x and divides; walking past the nearest such multiple is never useful. Memoized recursion f(v) handles the few interesting states.
k: If v <= y, the answer is simply y − v (only increments help).
Otherwise consider: all decrements (v − y), or move up/down to the nearest multiple of 11 (or 5), divide, and recurse.
Memoization bounds states: each division shrinks v by ≥5, so the recursion tree is tiny.

a.i: f(v) returns min ops from v to y. Base: v <= y → y − v. Else take the min of: v − y (pure decrements), (v mod 11) + 1 + f(v div 11), (11 − v mod 11) + 1 + f(v div 11 + 1), and the analogous pair for 5, plus 1 + f(v − 1).
s: Base case v <= y returns y − v.
Recurse on the five branches listed above; cache results.
a.t: O(log x · poly) — each branch divides v by ≥5, so recursion depth is logarithmic with constant branching.
a.sp: O(number of visited states) — memo entries, well under a few thousand.

w: Why branching only at multiples is safe: between consecutive multiples of 5 (or 11) the only useful moves are ±1 toward one endpoint or straight decrements toward y; anything else is dominated. Check examples: 26→1 = 3, 54→2 = 4, 25→30 = 5 (base case handles x < y). Alternative: BFS over states up to ~x+11 — also fine at these bounds. Follow-up: different divisors, or minimum-cost operations with weights.
